implementation_notes: cppzmq maps libzmq's C API onto RAII C++ types, so the endpoint is a small class owning zmq::context_t and one or more zmq::socket_t that exchange zmq::message_t frames: bind/connect the socket for the role, drive receive with a socket-blocking call or zmq::poll(), and use send_multipart/recv_multipart for multipart envelopes. The classic endpoint object survives, but its messaging half is the socket plus the poll loop, and ownership is the design problem: sockets are not thread-safe, so each socket stays with one thread.
pitfalls: ZeroMQ sockets are not thread-safe: create, use and close each socket on one thread, or transfer ownership with a full memory barrier (never share concurrently).
Declare the context before the sockets it owns; destroying a context while sockets are alive is undefined behaviour, and RAII only helps if declaration order matches the required lifetime.

variants.name: AMQP-CPP asynchronous channel callbacks (RabbitMQ)
variants.implementation_notes: AMQP-CPP is fully asynchronous and does not block: nearly every Channel method returns a Deferred on which you install onSuccess/onError callbacks, and consuming means channel.consume(queue).onReceived(cb).onSuccess(...).onCancelled(...).onError(...) with channel.ack(deliveryTag) and Channel::setQos() for prefetch. Choose it when the broker is RabbitMQ, C++17 is available and the application already has an event loop; prefer cppzmq when the transport should stay broker-agnostic or the toolchain stops at C++11.
pitfalls: Never run blocking work inside onReceived: the single handler thread also services the connection, so a long handler stalls consumption and the heartbeat.
A consumer can be cancelled by the broker (for example when the queue is removed); without the onCancelled handler the endpoint silently stops receiving.
